parts.title: Test that every feature works
parts.intro: Run these on the real site with a fresh account, the way a new customer would. A feature that works on a developer's laptop with three years of their own data in it is not the same as a feature that works.

sections.title: Getting into Scout
sections.blurb: If someone cannot sign up, nothing else on this page matters.

items.title: Sign up with an email address never used before
items.good: The verification code arrives within a minute or so, it is six digits, and the app accepts it.
steps: Open the site in a private or incognito window.
Sign up with an address nobody has used on Scout before.
Wait for the email, enter the code, and confirm you land inside the app.
If no email arrives at all, that is a broken, not a needs-work.
items.tech: Codes are generated by Supabase and sent through Resend over custom SMTP. The code input accepts exactly six characters, so an eight-digit code setting makes signup impossible.

items.title: Sign up again with an address that already has an account
items.good: You are taken to the sign-in screen with a clear message, rather than left waiting on a verify screen for an email that will never arrive.
steps: Try to sign up using an address you already registered.
Confirm you are told the account exists and routed to sign in.
items.tech: Supabase deliberately sends nothing on a repeat signup to avoid leaking which addresses are registered. The app has to detect this and redirect.

items.title: Reset a forgotten password
items.good: A reset code arrives, the new password is accepted, and you can sign in with it straight away.
steps: Use forgot password on a real test account.
Enter the emailed code and set a new password.
Sign out and sign back in with the new one.

items.title: Sign in on a second device and find everything there
items.good: Your profile, projects, and saved work all appear. Nothing has to be re-entered.
steps: Set up an account on a laptop.
Sign in to the same account on a phone.
Check the profile, projects, and any saved lists are all present.
items.tech: This is the failure the profile-saving migration exists to fix. If it is missing, saves fail silently and everything looks fine until you sign in elsewhere.

items.title: Stay signed in works the way it says
items.good: Ticking remember me keeps you signed in after closing the browser. Leaving it unticked does not.
steps: Sign in with remember me on, close the browser, reopen.
Repeat with it off and confirm the difference.

items.title: Switching between two saved accounts
items.good: You can flip between accounts without re-typing a password, and you never see the other account's data.
steps: Add two accounts.
Switch between them and confirm the finds, projects, and profile change completely each time.

items.title: Signing out really signs you out
items.good: After signing out, pressing back does not show the previous account's data.
steps: Sign out.
Press the browser back button several times.
Confirm you see the sign-in screen, not a stale copy of the app.

items.title: One-click Continue as keeps working day after day
items.good: Sign in, spend time in the app AND the admin pages, come back the next day signed out: 'Continue as' signs you straight in, no 'saved session expired' loop. If it does fail once, the error names the reason and your email is prefilled so recovery is one password.

items.title: A bad boot can't wipe your profile
items.good: If the profile/state load times out or fails, Scout lets you in but HOLDS all server writes for that session, an all-blank profile can never overwrite a filled row (server-side guard too), and blank server fields never shadow real local ones on merge. Kaitlyn's profile was wiped this way on 2026-08-24 and restored.

sections.title: Setting up for the first time
sections.blurb: The first ten minutes decide whether someone comes back. Test this with a genuinely empty account.

items.title: A brand new empty account looks welcoming, not broken
items.good: Empty screens explain what goes there and what to do next. No zeroes with no context, no blank panels, no error messages.
steps: Sign up fresh and look at every tab before doing anything: dashboard, finds, lists, templates.
Note anything that looks like a bug rather than an invitation.

items.title: Onboarding for a personal account
items.good: The questions make sense, the answers are saved, and what you typed visibly shapes what Scout suggests next.
steps: Go through onboarding as an individual.
Then check the profile screen and confirm your answers are actually stored there.

items.title: Onboarding for a company or team account
items.good: Same as above, plus the team features appear afterwards.
steps: Sign up a second fresh account and pick the company path.
Confirm the team tab is now available and pre-filled with the company details you gave.

items.title: The suggested starting projects are actually relevant
items.good: Scout suggests projects and search categories that match what you described, not generic filler like coffee chats.
steps: During setup, describe something specific, for example a student org booking speakers for a spring showcase.
Check the suggestions reference that, not a generic template.
items.tech: Generated by the starter plan route from the profile text.

items.title: Your profile still exists tomorrow
items.good: Fill in the profile, close everything, come back the next day, and it is all still there.
steps: Complete the profile fully.
Sign out, wait, sign back in.
Confirm nothing has to be re-entered.

items.title: Uploading a resume or bio fills in the right fields
items.good: It pulls out the name and a likely use case, leaves blank anything it cannot find, and never makes something up.
steps: Upload a real resume.
Check every pre-filled field against the document.
Anything invented is a broken, not a needs-work.

items.title: The walkthrough makes sense to someone who has never seen Scout
items.good: A person who did not build this can follow it without asking questions.
steps: Sit someone outside the team in front of it.
Do not help them. Write down every place they hesitate.

items.title: Voice dictation works where it is offered
items.good: The mic button appears only in browsers that support it, and dictated text lands in the right field.
steps: Try it in Chrome, then in a browser that does not support it, and confirm it hides rather than erroring.

items.title: Naming a project retunes its starter categories
items.good: A project named for a different world (say, Grad School) gets starter categories about that world, not leftovers from your last project.
steps: Create a project called something clearly different from your usual work, like Grad School.
Give it a one-line description and click out of the box.
Check the category list now suggests searches that fit the new project.
items.tech: New projects used to inherit the previous project's use case, which is why a Grad School project could open with Sync & Licensing.

items.title: You can delete the last project
items.good: Deleting your only project is allowed; Scout drops you into a fresh blank one instead of refusing.
steps: On a test account, delete every project.
Confirm you end up on a clean Untitled project rather than an error.

items.title: A search only auto-creates a category when it adds something
items.good: Running the project-level search, or a goal nearly identical to the project description or an existing category, does not mint a redundant category. A genuinely new goal still saves itself.
steps: Run the default project search; check Projects for a new near-duplicate category (fail if one appears).
Type a clearly different goal and run it; that one SHOULD appear as a category.
The Settings toggle (Searching section) turns auto-creation off entirely.

items.title: Solo Search is not mistaken for the run button
items.good: The Scout button is much bigger than the Solo Search pill; nobody taps Solo Search expecting to start a search.
steps: Show the Scout tab to someone new and ask them to start a search.
They should press the big cream Scout button on the first try.

items.title: Dictation shows your words as you speak
items.good: Pressing Dictate shows the live transcript on the button so it never looks dead.
steps: Press Dictate, speak a sentence, watch the words appear while speaking.

items.title: Add your LinkedIn lands on the adding step
items.good: The dashboard checklist's Add your LinkedIn button opens Profile AND scrolls to the resume/LinkedIn drop zone, not just the top of the tab.
steps: Click Add your LinkedIn from the dashboard checklist.
You should arrive with the upload area centred on screen.

items.title: Templates is three pages behind one toggle
items.good: Outreach, Application materials, and Email signatures are separate pages switched at the top — no scrolling between worlds. Cover letters are written, uploaded, or pasted IN Application materials; the outreach builder is not involved.
steps: Flip through all three pages.
Write and upload a cover letter without leaving Application materials.

items.title: Your links prefill from the profile
items.good: The Your links card starts filled with what Scout already knows (LinkedIn, account email, site/phone when present) and stays editable; nothing you typed is ever overwritten. Every kit surfaces them with copy buttons.
steps: On a fresh device, open Application materials and confirm the prefill.
Edit one, reload, confirm your edit stuck.

items.title: Templates can mint a project on the spot
items.good: In Templates' Where-it-applies picker (a house-styled dropdown, not the OS menu), '+ New project…' opens an inline name field; Create makes the project and scopes the template to it in one motion, same as Add-a-contact.

items.title: Profile splits into About you / Your company
items.good: On a company account, Profile is two pages behind a top toggle: your role and experience on one, the company details and color on the other. No scrolling through the company card to reach your own fields.

sections.title: Finding the right people
sections.blurb: The core promise of the product. If results are thin or made up, nothing downstream matters.

items.title: Scout shows it understood your goal before it searches
items.good: Before spending a search, it reflects back what it thinks you are looking for, and you recognise your own request in it.
steps: Type a goal and watch what it says it understood.
Confirm this pass does not count against your search allowance.
items.tech: The understanding pass decomposes the goal only, with no searching and no metering.

items.title: It asks a question when the goal is genuinely vague
items.good: A vague request gets one or two clarifying questions, not a shrug and a bad search.
steps: Type something deliberately thin, for example find me people in music.
Confirm you are asked something useful before it runs.

items.title: A real search for each of the three main use cases
items.good: Networking, job and internship hunting, and music PR each return people you would genuinely contact.
steps: Run one real search per use case.
For each, count how many of the top ten you would actually reach out to.
Under three out of ten is a needs-work.

items.title: A goal that fits none of the three templates still works
items.good: We promise Scout adapts to any free-text use case, so a request outside the templates has to produce sensible results.
steps: Type a goal from a completely different world, for example finding wedding venues or local suppliers.
Judge the results the same way.

items.title: The people it finds are real and the details are right
items.good: Names, roles, outlets, and links all check out when you click through.
steps: Take five results at random.
Click every link and verify the person holds that role at that place.
Any invented person or wrong role is a broken.

items.title: The reason it gives for each match is true
items.good: The why it fits line refers to something you can confirm on the linked page, not a plausible-sounding guess.
steps: For five results, read the reason and then try to confirm it from the source.
Flag anything that sounds specific but cannot be traced.

items.title: Fit scores sort good from bad
items.good: The high scoring results really are better than the low scoring ones. If the order is random, the score is worse than useless.
steps: Rank the top ten yourself without looking at the scores.
Compare your order with Scout's.

items.title: No duplicates, and no repeats of people you already have
items.good: The same person does not appear twice in one search, and does not come back in the next search either.
steps: Run the same search twice and compare.
Look for near-duplicates too, for example the same person under two spellings.

items.title: Typing a short category name produces a sensible search
items.good: Typing something like radio DJs or panelists gives Scout enough to find the right people, using your profile for context.
steps: Add two or three categories by name only.
Check the goal it writes for each one is specific and correct.

items.title: A deeper scan on one result adds real information
items.good: It returns facts you did not already have, all traceable to a source.
steps: Run it on someone you already know a lot about.
Check the new facts are both true and new.

items.title: Website previews load for results
items.good: The preview shows the actual site, quickly, without breaking the page.
steps: Scroll a full page of results with previews on.
Note any that hang, come back blank, or slow the page down.

items.title: A contact stops being suggested once several users have pitched them
items.good: Once a handful of different Scout users have reached out to the same person, that person stops appearing for everyone else.
steps: Ask a developer to confirm the cap is switched on and to show it working with test data.
This is the difference between an outreach tool and a spam tool, so it is worth proving rather than assuming.
items.tech: Backed by the shared contact ledger. It only works once the exposure table exists in the production database.

items.title: Passing on results changes what comes back
items.good: After you pass on several results for the same reason, the next search shows fewer like them.
steps: Pass on five results and give the same reason each time.
Run a similar search and see whether the pattern is gone.

items.title: A slow search keeps you company
items.good: Long runs show real progress, so the app never looks frozen.
steps: Run a big search on a slow connection.
Confirm something on screen keeps changing and tells you what is happening.

items.title: A search that finds nothing explains itself
items.good: You are told why and given something to try, not shown an empty box.
steps: Search for something deliberately impossible.
Read what you are told and decide whether it would help a real user.

items.title: Website previews require being signed in
items.good: Signed in, previews load fast and can be resized with the drag bar under them. Signed out, the preview area shows a polite sign-in page with a direct link to the site.
steps: Open a find while signed in and confirm the preview loads and the drag bar resizes it.
Copy the preview address into a private window and confirm it asks you to sign in instead of showing the site.
items.tech: The preview used to be an open proxy anyone on the internet could route traffic through; it now needs a short-lived signed pass that only signed-in users get.

items.title: A find's website is the real website
items.good: New finds never list a Yelp or YellowPages listing page as the company's site. If no real site is known, the field is empty and the listing stays under evidence.
steps: Run a search for local companies.
Click each Website field and confirm it goes to the company itself, not a review or directory page.

items.title: Hand-added contacts steer the next search
items.good: After you add a few people by hand, the next search in that project leans toward more people like them.
steps: Manually add two or three contacts of a very specific type.
Run a search and judge whether the results moved toward that type.

items.title: The shared index helps without making everyone's results the same
items.good: Searches quietly reuse people Scout has already verified, but two accounts running the same goal still get clearly different result sets, and fresh-from-the-web people always make up the majority.
steps: Open two browsers (or one normal + one private window): your account in one, a second account (Suri's, or a fresh signup) in the other.
Run the SAME goal text on both within a few minutes, e.g. 'indie playlist curators who take bedroom pop submissions'.
Put the two Finds lists side by side and compare names: mostly different people with some overlap is correct; near-identical lists is Broken.

Spot-check both lists: most finds should cite a live page (source link opens and mentions them), which is what fresh-from-the-web looks like. Every reused one still needs a true, checkable reason it fits THIS goal.
items.tech: Index candidates are capped at a small minority per search, sampled differently per user, expire from rotation after 90 days, and pass the same fit scoring and exposure caps as fresh candidates.

items.title: People-goals run as networking even in a job project
items.good: A goal about alumni, mentors, or people open to a chat returns PEOPLE with strong fits, never the 'few active postings matched' banner, even when the project is about applying to programs or jobs.
steps: In a job/grad-school project, search for alumni open to a coffee chat.
Confirm results are people with real fit scores, not employers or postings.
The word 'outlets' or a postings banner on a people-search is a broken.
items.tech: The goal text overrides the project's use case when it unambiguously asks for people, not openings.

items.title: People-searches sweep public LinkedIn profiles
items.good: An alumni or professionals search returns several results whose contact route is a LinkedIn profile, pulled from LinkedIn's public pages, not just news articles and school spotlights.
steps: Run a people-search (alumni of a program, professionals in a niche).
Count how many results carry a LinkedIn profile link.
Zero LinkedIn results on a clearly people-shaped search is a needs-work.
items.tech: Dedicated search queries scoped to linkedin.com; public pages only, no login.

items.title: Searches sweep the right platforms for the goal
items.good: The progress log names the platforms it swept, and they fit the request: alumni searches sweep LinkedIn and university pages, music searches sweep music profiles and Instagram, developer searches sweep GitHub, press searches sweep journalist sites. A wedding-venue search should not be sweeping music sites.
steps: Run searches in two very different worlds and watch the progress lines.
Confirm the platforms named make sense for each.
A music sweep on a non-music search is a needs-work.
items.tech: Up to three platform sweeps per search, chosen from the goal text; public pages only, no logins.

items.title: Roster searches reach people with no web footprint
items.good: A search naming a specific school, employer, or job title returns people the open web would never surface, with real names, roles, companies, and LinkedIn profiles. The progress log says it checked the people directory and how many match.
steps: Search for alumni of a named school, or people with a named job title.
Confirm you get names beyond the handful with press coverage.
Vague goals with no hard filter should skip the directory entirely, that is correct, not a bug.
items.tech: Licensed people directory (People Data Labs) queried only when the goal names a school, company, title, or industry; results pass the same fit and exposure gates as web finds.

items.title: A company's home base pulls nearby results up without hiding the rest
items.good: With a base set, results in that region come first, and strong matches elsewhere still appear further down rather than vanishing.
steps: Set a company location, for example Seattle, and run a search whose targets are national.
Confirm nearby results rank near the top.
Confirm results from elsewhere are still present, not filtered out.
Change the goal to say remote or anywhere, and confirm the location stops steering the results.
Clear the field and confirm searches behave as they did before.
items.tech: The base is passed to the planner as a preference, and the prompt tells it to put the wider region in preferred and weight proximity in ranking_factors, never a hard_constraint. If matches outside the region disappear entirely, the model is treating it as a filter and the wording needs tightening.

items.title: A search with no location given is not steered to any city
items.good: Results sit wherever the best matches are. No single city or region dominates, and nothing in the plan mentions a place nobody typed.
steps: Use an account with no location in the profile and no company base set.
Run a search whose goal names no place at all, for example people in the sports industry to talk to.
Read where the results are actually based. They should be spread out, not clustered in one metro.
Repeat on a second fresh account to be sure it is not one profile carrying a stale value.
If one region keeps winning, check whether any city is named in the planner prompt itself.
items.tech: This regressed once already: the HOME BASE rule in DECOMPOSE_SYS illustrated widening a region with real place names, and since they were the only cities in the prompt, goals with no location borrowed them as a default. The rule is now written without any place names, and says outright that with no base stated, location stays out of required, preferred, hard_constraints and ranking_factors. Empty location must mean no geography, not a fallback.

items.title: Setting a location narrows results as much as you meant it to
items.good: You have decided, deliberately, how strict a location should be, and what the app does matches that decision.
steps: Set a profile or company location, then run a search whose best matches are mostly elsewhere.
Count how many out-of-area results survive.
Try one in the same state but a different metro, and confirm it is treated the way you intend.
Decide whether that strictness is what you want, and change the scoring rule if it is not.
items.tech: Two stages disagree today. The planner treats a base as a soft preference (wider region in preferred, proximity weighted in ranking_factors). The extract prompt's LOCATION ALIGNMENT clause is far harsher: anything outside the exact metro is pinned to a fit_score of 0.01, and same-state-different-metro counts as a mismatch. So the soft preference described at plan time is overridden at scoring time. Pick one behavior and make both stages say it.

items.title: Scout asks where the work happens before searching for a role
items.good: A role-shaped search that never says remote or on-site pauses to ask, with one-tap answers, and the answer visibly changes who comes back.
steps: Search for a kind of role without saying anything about where the work happens.
Confirm Scout asks about remote, hybrid, or on-site before running.
Answer it and confirm the results reflect the answer.
Run a search that already says remote, and confirm Scout does NOT ask again.
Re-run a search you have already answered, and confirm it is not asked twice.
items.tech: The planner caps understanding at 85 for a role-shaped goal with no work arrangement stated, which keeps it under the gate that would otherwise run the search silently. A category that scored 100 on an earlier run used to bury this; the gate now uses the current read whenever there are open questions. Answered questions are banked so they are never re-asked.

items.title: Nobody reaches your pipeline without a way to contact them
items.good: Every find has an email, a phone number, or a handle. Not one is a bio page with no way to get in touch.
steps: Run a few searches across different use cases, including one for a sport, a league, or a club.
Open each find and confirm it carries a real email, phone number, or handle.
A profile or bio page on its own does not count. If one of those is showing, the rule is not holding.
Open the skipped list for the run and confirm the drops read "no way to contact them".
Try a roster or staff-directory search, the kind where pages list names and nothing else, and confirm those names do not come through.
items.tech: The gate is in discover(), keyed on an actual contact value — contactEmail, contactPhone or contactHandle — never on the channel field, which is only the extractor's guess at a route and gets set to things like "Website Form" on results carrying no contact detail at all. That loophole is how a Reign FC player with only a bio page once got through. The gate runs after the Phase 2 enrichment pass so anyone whose address was about to be found still gets that chance.

items.title: The contact rule has not quietly starved the results
items.good: Searches still come back with a useful number of people. When one is thin, the skipped list explains why rather than leaving it looking broken.
steps: Run the searches you would actually run and note how many finds each returns.
Compare against what the same search used to give you.
For a thin one, open the skipped list and count how many were dropped for having no contact.
If good people are being lost rather than genuinely unreachable ones, raise the enrichment budget instead of relaxing the rule.
items.tech: Requiring a contact route necessarily returns fewer people, which is the intended trade. The lever is the Phase 2 enrichment pass in discover(): it chases contacts for only six finds per search to stay inside the time budget, prioritizing those with no contact at all since they are the ones facing deletion. Raising that six recovers people without loosening the rule, at the cost of a slower search.

items.title: Starring a find moves it to the top in your own color
items.good: The star fills with the color set in the profile, the find jumps to the top of the list, and it is still counted in its status tab rather than disappearing from it.
steps: Open Finds and star something near the bottom of the list.
Confirm it moves straight to the top and the star fills in.
Check the star's color matches the one picked in Profile, then change that color and confirm the star follows.
Confirm the status counts along the top did not drop — starring marks a find, it does not move it out of New or Sent.
Star two or three, and confirm they sit together at the top in the order you starred them.
Reload the page and confirm the stars and the order survive.
Change the sort and confirm starred finds still lead.
items.tech: Starred finds are sorted to the front after the chosen sort is applied, so the sort still orders everything below them. This replaced the old pushpin, which pulled a find OUT of its status list into a separate Pinned tab; the tab remains as a filter for seeing only starred finds. The star's color is set inline from --c-brown, the brand token a chosen accent overrides — it was set via the text-accent class first, which is on the element but loses somewhere in the row's cascade and rendered muted grey.

items.title: Job searches return openings and employers, never bare people
items.good: On a job or internship search, every result is either a specific posting or a company you could approach. No plain LinkedIn profiles or staff bios of people who merely work somewhere.
steps: Run a job-type search (the Work Opportunities project works).
Scan the results: anything that is just a person's profile with no opening attached is a fail.
A recruiter is fine only when named as the contact ON a specific opening.

items.title: Every scout brings back at least five results
items.good: A search never comes back with one or two finds. Under five, Scout widens on its own and fills the rest with fittable employers to cold-email, and a banner says plainly that those are not confirmed openings.
steps: Run a narrow search where live postings are scarce.
Count the results: five or more.
Read the banner over the results and confirm it explains any cold-outreach fallback.

items.title: A deny reason that names an unwanted world is a hard filter
items.good: After denying with a reason like 'I don't want to work in country music', later searches never surface results squarely in that world, not even as low-fit.
steps: Deny a find with a reason naming a genre or industry you don't want.
Run two or three more searches in that category.
Confirm nothing from that world comes back.

items.title: Timing denies go on a reopen watch, not a blocklist
items.good: Denying with 'no open positions' does not banish the company. It can come back occasionally as a check-in, and comes back prominently when it actually has a live opening, saying positions have opened since you last checked.
steps: Deny a company with the reason 'No open positions'.
Run several searches over following days.
Confirm it is not gone forever, and that any return without an opening is labeled as a re-check.

items.title: The detail rail answers your own criteria as fields
items.good: Opening a new find shows static labeled rows answering the goal's explicit asks: Remote? In person, Vancouver. Paid? Not stated. Answers come from the source; silent sources say Not stated, never a guess.
steps: Run a search whose goal states criteria (remote or in person, paid, timeframe).
Open a NEW find (old finds predate this) and check the left rail above Why it fits.
Verify each answer against the actual page.

items.title: Eligibility requirements you cannot meet disqualify a find
items.good: A program that requires an affiliation the profile clearly lacks (a specific school, members only, residency) never shows up as a fit. When you DO meet a stated requirement, Why it fits says so.
steps: Search with a profile that names your school/location.
Look for any find whose page limits participation to a group the profile is not in.
Finding one scored as a fit is a fail (the UBC mentor program bug).

items.title: Scout knows when companies post and recommends first
items.good: The shared index remembers stated posting windows ('Opens each January') and the months live postings were seen, and searches check an org right as its window opens.
steps: Hard to test directly; spot-check that a find whose page states an application window shows it in the criteria rows.
Over time, watch whether recurring programs (annual internships) resurface at the right time of year.
items.tech: Cadence lives on the people_index rows (postingWindow + postingMonths in the opp JSON) and feeds the query planner's index compass with the current month.

items.title: Handshake pages appear when they are public
items.good: Job searches sweep joinhandshake.com. Yield is thin by design: Handshake walls most postings behind login and Scout only sees public pages.
steps: Run a student-flavored job search and look for any joinhandshake.com results.
None appearing is acceptable; a login page appearing as a find is a fail.

items.title: Refreshing the page stops a running scout
items.good: Closing or refreshing the tab aborts the search server-side instead of burning credits in the background.
steps: Start a search, refresh mid-run.
Confirm the run does not keep producing finds afterward.

items.title: The progress log stays readable
items.good: The live search log spreads side to side, clips long queries, and if the same status line would print again back-to-back it prints once with a count (like 'Skipped a duplicate (x4)') instead of repeating. It never grows past the screen.
steps: Start a search and watch the progress card.
Confirm two columns on a wide screen and no line running off the card.

items.title: Scouting shows honest live timers
items.good: Under the reading deck: Time saving leads at display size, with 'Xm scouting vs Ym doing these searches yourself' beneath. The manual estimate is computed from the run's real counts with research-backed rates: 30s per web search (eye-tracking puts picking a result at ~9s, plus typing and reformulating; Mediative 2014, Granka et al.) and 60s per site opened (Nielsen Norman Group: average page visit just under a minute). The tooltip shows the formula — nothing invented.
steps: Run a search and watch the numbers move.
Hover the block and check the formula matches the run's own search/site counts.

items.title: Variety searches rotate industries run over run
items.good: When a goal welcomes many industries, back-to-back scouts don't find the same field twice: the planner reads which industries past keeps already cover and points the new run at ones not yet represented.
steps: On a variety goal, run two scouts in a row and compare the industries of the results.

items.title: The scarcity rescue reaches the five-find floor
items.good: A run still short after widening plans fresh queries that deliberately span the other industries the goal allows, and accepts honest moderate fits (never inflated scores). The log says 'Only N so far; widening into other industries to reach 5.'
steps: Run a narrow search where the specific ask runs dry.
Confirm at least five results, the log line, and that rescue results carry honest moderate fit bands.

items.title: Deleted finds come back
items.good: Deleting a find drops it into 'Show recently deleted' at the foot of Finds (this device). Bring it back restores it exactly as it was, draft and status intact; Delete forever really removes it.

items.title: Find tiles read as Scout, not as brand slabs
items.good: Grid tiles paint a soft pastel of the site's brand color with the logo or dog in the deepened color itself. No full-strength color blocks, and a find with no known color gets a pastel from the field deck, never a dead grey tile.

items.title: Spreadsheet junk can't haunt the grid
items.good: Old imports that let FALSE/TRUE cells or bare ids through as names get scrubbed on load; anything left nameless moves to recently deleted (recoverable), so no more FALSE cards or id-titled tiles.

sections.title: The application desk
sections.blurb: Applying well is half the product now. Every item here is about the Applications tab and its kits.

items.title: Only real application prospects reach the desk
items.good: The Applications tab holds things you APPLY to. People (coordinators, professors, contacts) never appear automatically, and a school name in the organization field alone does not qualify a find.
steps: Open Applications on a pipeline that includes networking contacts.
Any bare person auto-listed is a fail; mark one by hand from its detail view and confirm it appears, untrack and it leaves.

items.title: Organized by your projects and categories
items.good: The toggles mirror your own structure: one chip per project (with counts), and picking a project reveals its categories as a second row. Filtering never loses anything; All brings it back.
steps: Click through the project chips and a category sub-chip.
Counts must add up, and All must always show everything.

items.title: Deadline first, full-width rows
items.good: The list is ordered by parsed deadline (soonest first, red under a week, 'no deadline found' honest when absent), one application per row across the screen.
steps: Add a posting with a stated deadline ('apply by …') and confirm it sorts above undated ones with the right date and days-left.
Rows must never sit two-across.

items.title: The kit walks you through the whole application
items.good: Opening a prospect is a full-screen, numbered walkthrough: (1) point of contact and your materials, (2) a cover letter tailored to THIS posting with minimal edits and bracketed fill-ins, (3) know-them research with interview prep — plus Open posting up top.
steps: Open a kit on a real posting.
Check the contact copies, the resume downloads, the letter reads as YOUR letter lightly edited, and the research cites real facts.

items.title: Paste a posting builds the prospect from nothing
items.good: Pasting a whole job description (Applications or Manual) parses role/org/contact, researches the organization, and lands the prospect in Finds and Applications with its kit ready.
steps: Paste a real posting from the web.
Confirm the created find carries the right role, org, and any stated contact, and opens a working kit.

items.title: Schools bring scholarship leads
items.good: When the target is a school or degree program, the kit's research includes real scholarship or aid leads with links — never fabricated ones.
steps: Build an application for a masters program.
Check each scholarship link actually resolves and relates.

items.title: Application files persist and match the moment
items.good: A file added during one application (a song, a portfolio) is kept and pulled up automatically the next time it fits — audio for playlist/music submissions, documents broadly. Files are grouped by kind in Templates > Application materials.
steps: Add a file from inside a kit; reload; open another kit of the same kind and confirm it surfaces.
Remove it from Application files and confirm it stays gone.

items.title: Compare charts a group with your own ranking
items.good: Compare view shows a type group side by side — location, the group's own criteria (tuition, paid, remote, deadline…), fit, status — with a My-rank column you type into that reorders the list.
steps: Switch a group with several prospects to Compare.
Set ranks 1-3 and confirm the ordering follows; clear a rank and it falls back to deadline order.

items.title: Cover letter mastery keeps your voice
items.good: Tailoring (in a kit or Templates > Application materials) proposes the SMALLEST spot edits: your sentences survive, truly incompatible passages are flagged for YOU to resolve, and suggestions never point at text that isn't in your letter.
steps: Run your real letter against a real posting.
Count the edits (should be a handful), verify each 'original' really is in your letter, and that Keep-my-original works.

items.title: Deadlines are editable in place
items.good: Clicking the deadline spot on any Applications row (or its 'set deadline' placeholder) opens the native date picker right there. A hand-set date wins over the parsed one and the list re-sorts immediately; clearing it falls back to the parsed date.
steps: Click a row's deadline, pick a date next week: it should turn red-ish with days-left and re-sort.
Clear it and confirm the parsed deadline (or 'set deadline') returns.

items.title: A kit can skip the cover letter
items.good: 'Don't need a cover letter' on a kit's cover-letter step removes that section for THIS application only (the next step renumbers), with a small link to bring it back. The choice sticks across reopens.
steps: Remove it on one application, close and reopen the kit: still gone.
Open a different application: its cover-letter step is untouched.

items.title: Research cites real sources
items.good: Know-them ends with Sources and recent news: the actual pages the research read, linked with their real titles. Every link resolves and relates; none are invented.
steps: Open a few links from one kit and confirm they're real, relevant pages about the organization.

items.title: Your links read as links, not stray files
items.good: In the kit's files column, saved links sit under their own 'Your links (what forms ask for)' heading with LINKEDIN / EMAIL / WEBSITE labels and copy buttons — never as unexplained bare values among the files.
steps: Open a kit with saved links and check the labeling.

items.title: Kit research talks to you, briefly
items.good: Know-them research says 'you' and 'your', never your name in the third person, and stays short: a couple of company facts, 2-3 before-you-apply points, 3-4 prep questions, one scannable line each.

sections.title: Bringing in your own lists
sections.blurb: Most people arrive with a spreadsheet already. This is where they decide whether Scout is for them.

items.title: Import a real, messy spreadsheet
items.good: It handles merged cells, blank rows, notes in odd places, and inconsistent headers without falling over.
steps: Use an actual working file, not a clean sample.
Check the imported rows against the file for anything dropped or scrambled.

items.title: Scout reads the columns correctly, or asks
items.good: It works out which column is a name, an email, or a company. When it is unsure, it asks rather than guessing.
steps: Import a file with unusual header names.
Check every column was mapped to the right thing.

items.title: Import from a Google Sheets link
items.good: Pasting a link imports the rows, and a link that is not shared gives a clear message about permissions.
steps: Import a shared sheet.
Then try one that is private and read the error.

items.title: Accents and unusual characters survive
items.good: Names with accents or non-English characters come through intact.
steps: Include names with accents in a test file.
Check them in the imported list and again in a draft message.
items.tech: Related to a known issue elsewhere where accented spellings were treated as different people.

items.title: A very large file does not hang the app
items.good: It either handles it or tells you the limit. It never spins forever.
steps: Try a file with several thousand rows.
Time it and note what the screen does while you wait.

items.title: A broken or wrong file fails politely
items.good: A corrupt file, or a photo renamed as a spreadsheet, produces a clear message and no damage.
steps: Rename an image to end in .csv and upload it.
Confirm you get a plain-English message and can carry on.

items.title: Adding a contact by hand
items.good: You can add someone manually with everything you know, and they behave exactly like a found result afterwards.
steps: Add one manually, then draft to them and confirm it works the same way.

items.title: Spreadsheet junk does not become contacts
items.good: Checkbox values like TRUE and FALSE never show up as names or LinkedIn handles, sentence-long notes are skipped instead of imported as people, and emails are found even when the email column was mislabeled.
steps: Import a messy sheet that has checkbox columns and note rows.
Confirm no row is named FALSE and no note-sentence became a contact.
Spot-check that emails present anywhere in a row were picked up.

items.title: Imported rows link back to the exact sheet row
items.good: A contact from a linked Google Sheet has a small open-in-sheet arrow that opens the source spreadsheet scrolled to that person's row.
steps: Open the Spreadsheet tab after a sheet sync.
Click the arrow next to an imported contact and confirm the right row is highlighted in Google Sheets.

items.title: Imported personal contacts stay private
items.good: After importing a spreadsheet, published business addresses (submissions@, booking@, info@) may help other accounts' searches, but a private individual's personal address (a gmail, a named person's work mailbox) never leaves your account.
steps: Import a sheet containing both a role inbox and a personal address.
Confirm both appear in your own pipeline.
The personal one must never surface in another account's search results.
items.tech: isBusinessContact gates what crosses into the shared index: role-style inboxes on non-freemail domains only.

items.title: A hand-added contact researches itself
items.good: Right after adding a contact by hand, Scout quietly runs the same public-web enrichment as Autofill: blank fields (role, outlet, link, location) fill in and the 'Added by you' placeholder becomes one real factual line when the web has one. Nothing invented; blanks stay blank when nothing is found.

items.title: A sheet's data actually lands on the finds
items.good: After importing a real tracking sheet, the rows carry the sheet's company, email, phone, and links, not blanks with placeholder text. Kaitlyn's current pipeline shows imported rows with empty contact fields, so this is under investigation.
steps: Re-import the sheet from Manual and watch the column-mapping step: does each column map to the right field?
Open a few imported finds and compare against the original sheet row by row.
If the mapping looks right but fields are still blank, mark Broken with the sheet's column names in the note.

items.title: A pasted posting files where you choose
items.good: Both Paste-a-posting boxes (Manual and Applications) offer project and category pickers; the built prospect lands exactly there, not in whatever project was active.

sections.title: Writing the messages
sections.blurb: The part users judge us on hardest. Read the drafts as if you were the person receiving them.

items.title: The first draft sounds like a person, not a template
items.good: You would be willing to send it with light edits. It does not open with generic flattery or read like every other outreach email.
steps: Generate five drafts for five different people.
Read them aloud.
Count how many you would send as-is.

items.title: Two drafts for two different people are obviously different
items.good: Swap the names between two drafts and it should immediately look wrong. If they are interchangeable, the personalisation is fake.
steps: Put two drafts side by side.
Swap the names and see whether anyone would notice.

items.title: No draft claims anything about the recipient we cannot back up
items.good: Every specific claim about their work traces back to something in the result, not to a guess.
steps: Take three drafts and highlight every factual claim.
Try to confirm each one from the source.
Anything unconfirmable is a broken.

items.title: Email gets a full message, a social handle gets a short note
items.good: The format matches the channel automatically, without you having to ask.
steps: Draft for one contact with an email and one with only a social handle.
Compare length and tone.

items.title: Editing a draft teaches Scout your voice
items.good: After you rewrite a few drafts heavily, later drafts start closer to how you write.
steps: Rewrite three drafts substantially in your own words.
Generate three more and see whether they moved toward you.

items.title: The writing coach comments on your actual messages
items.good: The advice quotes your real drafts and says something specific. Generic outreach tips are a needs-work.
steps: Ask for advice after writing several messages.
Check it refers to things you actually wrote.

items.title: Follow-up drafts remember the first message
items.good: The follow-up reads like a second message to the same person, not a fresh cold email.
steps: Draft a first message, then a follow-up.
Read them in sequence as the recipient would.

items.title: Redrafting a batch at once
items.good: Redoing several drafts together produces the same quality as doing them one at a time, and nothing gets mixed up between people.
steps: Redraft ten at once.
Check every one is still addressed to the right person with the right details.

items.title: The application writer produces something submittable
items.good: Given a real job posting, the cover letter and answers are specific to that posting and to the applicant.
steps: Paste a real internship posting.
Read the output as if you were the hiring manager.

items.title: House writing rules are respected
items.good: No em dashes anywhere, no filler openings, no exclamation marks unless you wrote them.
steps: Scan ten drafts for the house rules.
One slip is a needs-work, a pattern is broken.

items.title: You choose which template a draft starts from
items.good: On a find with two or more templates in scope, the Draft button grows a 'Best template (auto)' picker listing each template by kind and first words. Picking one drafts from that voice alone; auto still matches by format.

items.title: One email link, not two
items.good: The find detail shows the address itself as the contact link; there is no separate Email chip repeating it (Call chip gone the same way).

items.title: Team templates can be deleted
items.good: A shared template row has Delete: your own delete removes it from the library (and your local copy so sync can't resurrect it); an admin can delete anyone's. A non-admin deleting someone else's gets a plain refusal, not a broken row.

sections.title: Sending
sections.blurb: The only part that touches a stranger's inbox. Mistakes here cost us our sending reputation, not just a bug report.

items.title: Connect a Gmail account
items.good: The connection completes on the live site and still works a week later.
steps: Connect a Gmail account on the real domain.
Come back a week later and confirm it is still connected.
items.tech: If the Google app is still in testing mode, only listed test users can connect and their access expires after seven days, so this looks fine on day one and breaks quietly later.

items.title: Connect an Outlook account
items.good: Same as Gmail, including for a work account with stricter settings.
steps: Connect a personal Outlook account, then a work one if you have access to one.

items.title: Draft-for-review mode versus send-directly mode
items.good: Whichever you choose, Scout does exactly that. In review mode nothing ever leaves without you pressing send.
steps: Set it to create drafts only and run the whole flow.
Check your sent folder and confirm nothing went out.

items.title: One real message, to a real inbox
items.good: It arrives, in the inbox rather than spam, and it looks right on a phone.
steps: Send to an address on a different provider from yours.
Check where it landed and how it renders on a phone.

items.title: Every message has a working unsubscribe
items.good: The link is in the received message, it works, and it says clearly what just happened.
steps: Open a received message and click the unsubscribe link.
Read the confirmation as a stranger would.

items.title: Unsubscribing actually stops future messages
items.good: After someone opts out, no further message from that account can reach them, including scheduled and automatic ones.
steps: Unsubscribe an address.
Try to send and schedule to it again.
This one is a legal problem if it fails, not just a bug.

items.title: Schedule a message and watch it go
items.good: It goes out at the time promised, once, and not twice.
steps: Schedule a message a short time ahead.
Wait and confirm exactly one copy arrives.

items.title: Sending respects working hours where the recipient is
items.good: Messages land during their working day, not the middle of their night.
steps: Schedule to contacts in two very different time zones.
Confirm both arrive at a sensible local hour.

items.title: An unknown or blank location falls back sensibly
items.good: A contact with no location still gets a reasonable send time rather than three in the morning somewhere.
steps: Schedule to a contact with the location left empty.
Note the time it chooses.

items.title: Someone who replied never gets the automatic follow-up
items.good: A real reply stops the sequence immediately.
steps: Send a message, reply from the other inbox.
Confirm the follow-up does not go out.

items.title: Disconnecting a mailbox stops everything queued for it
items.good: Disconnecting revokes access and cancels anything waiting to send from that account.
steps: Queue several scheduled messages.
Disconnect the mailbox.
Confirm none of them ever arrive.

items.title: A failed send is visible and fixable
items.good: If a message fails, you can see it failed and why, and try again.
steps: Send to a deliberately invalid address.
Look for where the failure surfaces in the app.

sections.title: Running on autopilot
sections.blurb: The riskiest feature we have, because it acts while nobody is watching.

items.title: Set up a recurring search
items.good: You can say what to look for and how often, and it runs on that schedule.
steps: Create one.
Confirm it actually runs at the next scheduled time, not just that it saved.

items.title: The digest email arrives and reads well on a phone
items.good: It is scannable, the results are clear, and the buttons are easy to tap.
steps: Open a real digest on a phone.
Try to act on it one-handed.

items.title: Approve and deny from the email without signing in
items.good: Tapping approve or deny works straight from the email and confirms what happened.
steps: Tap both, on a phone, while signed out.

items.title: An old or tampered link is refused
items.good: Editing the link, or using a very old one, gets a clear refusal rather than acting on someone else's account.
steps: Change a character in the link and open it.
Confirm you get a refusal, not an action.

items.title: Nothing is ever sent without a person approving it
items.good: There is no path, including a double click or a reused link, that gets a message out without human approval.
steps: Walk the whole automatic flow and try to break the approval step.
Try clicking approve twice and confirm only one message goes out.

items.title: Turning autopilot off stops everything
items.good: Switching it off cancels pending searches, drafts, and sends, immediately.
steps: Turn it off with work queued.
Wait through the next scheduled run and confirm nothing happened.

sections.title: Getting smarter over time
sections.blurb: We promise Scout improves. That promise needs to be visible, and one part of it needs a decision before launch.

items.title: Decide whether the self-editing job stays on at launch
items.good: This is a decision, not a test. A nightly job reads how people are rating results and then edits our own live code and publishes it, with no human reviewing the change first.
steps: Agree as a team whether that runs on launch day.
The safer version is to have it propose the change and have a person approve it.
If it stays on, everyone should know how to spot and undo a bad change.
items.tech: The nightly tuning job commits directly to the main branch through a scoped access token. Its safety net is that it may only replace the contents of specific named clauses, not arbitrary code.

items.title: The reasons people give for passing are grouped sensibly
items.good: Three differently worded versions of wrong industry count as one reason, not three.
steps: Pass on results using slightly different wordings of the same reason.
Check the summary counts them together.

items.title: Scout visibly gets better within one session
items.good: After a round of passes and edits, the next batch is noticeably closer to what you want.
steps: Score the first ten results out of ten.
Do a round of passing and editing, then score the next ten.

items.title: Community comparisons can never point at one person
items.good: Any people like you statistic is an average over enough other users that nobody can be identified.
steps: Ask a developer to confirm the minimum group size and show what happens below it.

items.title: The insights screen matches reality
items.good: The numbers on it agree with what you can count yourself.
steps: Pick two numbers and verify them by hand against the underlying rows.

sections.title: Keeping track of the pipeline
sections.blurb: The dashboard's whole job is to be trusted. A confidently wrong number is worse than no number.

items.title: Dashboard numbers match reality
items.good: Every count on the dashboard can be verified by hand against the actual rows.
steps: Pick three numbers.
Count the underlying items yourself.
Any mismatch is a broken, however small.

items.title: Statuses stick
items.good: Marking something as sent or replied survives a reload and shows up on the dashboard.
steps: Change several statuses, reload, and check the dashboard moved.

items.title: List and grid views of finds
items.good: Both views show the same items, sort the same way, and stay usable with hundreds of rows.
steps: Switch between views with a large set of finds.
Check the counts match in both.

items.title: Saved lists survive a reload
items.good: A saved list is still there after a refresh, and after signing in somewhere else.
steps: Save a list, reload, then check it on another device.

items.title: Deep links land on the right row
items.good: Clicking a link through to a spreadsheet row opens the right row, not the top of the sheet.
steps: Try several from different lists.

items.title: Writing results out to Google Sheets
items.good: The rows land in the right sheet, in the right columns, without overwriting anything.
steps: Write to a sheet that already has data in it.
Confirm nothing existing was damaged.

items.title: Your own pass reasons become one-tap options
items.good: After you type a custom reason for passing on a find, it appears as a tappable chip next time, most-used first.
steps: Pass on a find and type a reason of your own.
Pass on another and confirm your reason is now a chip you can tap.

items.title: Finds can be filtered by where they came from
items.good: The Finds tab has a Scout-found / Manual / Both toggle, defaulting to Scout-found, and the counts always match the list shown.
steps: On an account with both kinds, open Finds.
Flip through all three settings and confirm the list and counts change together.

items.title: Lists give an outsider a clear status board
items.good: A list (say, Band members) shows everyone in plain English: not contacted yet, reached out with the date, replied, passed. Someone who has never used Scout can read it cold.
steps: Create a list from the Lists tab for one project or category.
Show it to someone outside the team and ask them who has been contacted.
Change a find's status elsewhere and confirm the list updates by itself.

items.title: The dashboard lives on the colour field
items.good: The dashboard ground is a soft blended colour field (a fresh trio of tints dealt every time you open it, never repeating its lead), with film grain on the ground only and frosted translucent cards in one consistent surface style.
steps: Open the dashboard several times; the field's colours must change each open.
Check buttons and text are clean (no grain speckle) and no card is plain solid white.

items.title: Time saved scouting is on the dashboard
items.good: The stat band shows hours saved (an estimate of manual sourcing plus drafting time), and it grows as finds accumulate.
steps: Check the dashboard band for 'Hours saved scouting'.
Sanity-check the number against roughly 15 minutes per find plus 10 per draft.

sections.title: Working as a team
sections.blurb: Built and reviewed, but never actually run with two real people. That has to happen before launch.

items.title: Two real people, one invite, one join
items.good: One person creates a workspace and invites, the other signs in, sees the invite, and joins successfully.
steps: Use two genuinely separate accounts on two machines.
Do not shortcut it with two tabs on one laptop.
items.tech: The repo notes say this flow has been type-checked and reviewed but never exercised with two signed-in users.

items.title: Sharing a project with the team
items.good: The shared project's finds appear for everyone on it, and only for them.
steps: Share a project with one teammate and not another.
Confirm the excluded person cannot see it.

items.title: Two people cannot claim the same contact
items.good: The second person is told it is already taken. Nobody gets pitched twice by the same company.
steps: Have both people click claim on the same contact at nearly the same time.

items.title: A viewer cannot do editor things
items.good: Someone with view-only access cannot change anything, even if they know the direct link.
steps: Sign in as a viewer and try to change a status and send an invite.
Ask a developer to confirm the refusal comes from the server, not just a hidden button.

items.title: Removing someone cuts their access immediately
items.good: Access ends the moment they are removed, not when they next sign out.
steps: Remove a member while they are actively using the app.
Have them try to load a shared project.

items.title: The team does not email the same person twice
items.good: If two teammates both have the same contact, only one message goes out.
steps: Put the same contact in two teammates' lists and run the automatic flow.

items.title: Invite and company codes cannot be guessed
items.good: The codes are long enough not to be brute-forced, and repeated wrong attempts are slowed down.
steps: Ask a developer to confirm the code length and whether attempts are limited.

items.title: Shared templates work for everyone
items.good: A template saved for the team is usable by every member and edits do not clash.
steps: Have two people use and edit the same template.

items.title: A co-owner can be promoted and not demoted
items.good: The owner can set a member's role to Co-owner. Once someone is an owner, nobody (including the other owner) can change or remove their role.
steps: As the owner, change a teammate's role to Co-owner in the Team tab.
As that co-owner, confirm you can manage admins.
Try to change the other owner's role from either account, it must refuse.

items.title: A find one teammate turns up shows up for the others
items.good: Someone else's find appears in your list under the same project it was found in, and under All projects, with their name on it.
steps: With two real accounts on the same team, have the first person run a search under a named project.
As the second person, open that same project and confirm the find is there.
Switch to All projects and confirm it is there too.
Confirm it does NOT appear under a different, unrelated project.
Have both people find the same person, and confirm they see one row rather than two.
items.tech: Searches publish through mergeFinds to /api/team/finds, which opens a shared project matching the local project's name on the first find. Rows dedup on (shared_project_id, dedup_key), where the key is name plus website host from lib/findKeys and is deliberately free of any project id. Two rows for one person means the key is being computed differently by two paths.

items.title: Someone who joins the team later still sees what was already found
items.good: A person invited after the searching happened opens the project and sees the finds already in it.
steps: On a team that already has finds, invite a fresh account and accept.
As the new person, open the project and confirm the earlier finds are visible.
items.tech: This is what open_to_workspace is for: membership rows are written when a project is created, so a later joiner has none. Access falls back to workspace membership on projects Scout opened automatically. Projects shared by hand keep their picked member list on purpose, so a later joiner will NOT see those.

items.title: You can see who found each find while scrolling
items.good: On a shared pipeline, grid cards carry a small chip with the finder's name next to the status, and the list view says 'Found by <name>' instead of a generic label.
steps: Open Finds on the team lens with the Everyone filter.
Scroll the grid: every teammate-found card names its finder without opening it.

items.title: Team news reads like sentences
items.good: The dashboard news card says things like 'anna found 12 new prospects in My outreach' and 'anna sent 5 messages', never jargon like 'moved outreach: sent 1000'.
steps: With a teammate active, open the dashboard news card and read each line as an outsider.

sections.title: Paying for it
sections.blurb: Test with a real card on the live site. Test mode proves nothing about launch day.

items.title: The free allowance matches what we advertise
items.good: The number of free searches in the product, on the pricing page, and in our documentation are all the same number.
steps: Count the free searches you actually get.
Compare against the pricing page and the setup docs.
items.tech: Right now the code allows three free searches per month while the setup documentation says five. Pick one and make everything agree.

items.title: Buy the Starter plan with a real card
items.good: Checkout completes, the plan shows as active, the allowance goes up straight away, and a receipt arrives.
steps: Buy it properly on the live site.
Watch the allowance change without needing a reload or a sign out.

items.title: Buy the Pro plan, and upgrade from Starter to Pro
items.good: Both work, and upgrading gives the higher allowance immediately without double charging.
steps: Buy Pro on one account, upgrade another from Starter.

items.title: Running out of searches is a clear next step, not an error
items.good: You are told what happened, when it resets, and how to get more. It should read like an offer, not a failure.
steps: Use up an account's allowance completely.
Read the screen as a new customer would.

items.title: Managing the subscription from inside the app
items.good: You can update a card, see invoices, and cancel without emailing us.
steps: Do all three from the billing screen.

items.title: Cancelling keeps access until the end of the paid month
items.good: Cancelling does not cut someone off the moment they click it.
steps: Cancel and confirm the access end date shown is the end of the paid period.

items.title: Two searches at the same time cannot cheat the limit
items.good: Someone on their last search cannot get two by starting them together.
steps: Open two tabs on an account with one search left and start both at once.

items.title: A free access code works once and only once
items.good: It grants access on the first account and is refused on the second.
steps: Redeem a code, then try the same code on another account.

items.title: A failed payment does not lock someone out mid-work
items.good: A card that fails gives a warning and a grace period, not an immediate wall.
steps: Ask a developer to simulate a failed renewal and watch what the user sees.

sections.title: Trials, and the tools only we can see
sections.blurb: The way people meet Scout before signing up, and the back office we use to help them.

items.title: Trying Scout without an account
items.good: The trial link runs a real search, and the path into signing up is obvious once it runs out.
steps: Open the trial link in a private window.
Use up the trial and see what you are offered.

items.title: Only the right people can reach the admin screens
items.good: An ordinary account cannot see or reach the admin area, even with the direct link.
steps: Sign in as a normal account and try the admin address directly.
Ask a developer to confirm the refusal comes from the server.

items.title: Running a search on someone's behalf
items.good: It works, the results land in their account, and there is a record of who did it and when.
steps: Seed results for a test account and sign in as that account to check.

items.title: Seeded results appear only for the intended person
items.good: Nobody else ever sees results prepared for someone else.

Read each message as a non-technical user.
